writing.explanation:
In ahishers, matches are his, she, he and hers, total 4. At the end of she, its failure chain also recognizes he. In aaaa with patterns a and aa, overlaps produce 4+3=7 matches.

The worked program is a complete executable for this pattern. Its core function uses typed input so the state transitions remain visible. The challenge input contract is: Parse lowercase ASCII text and nonempty lowercase ASCII patterns. Count every pattern occurrence, including overlaps and simultaneous suffix matches. The visible fixture is `text=ahishers patterns=[he,she,his,hers]` and its example result is `4`. The implementation and additional semantic fixtures were checked against an independent reference calculation. Those bounded tests establish these examples; they are not a proof for all inputs or a measurement on an iPhone.

Return a canonical String from solve: lowercase true/false for booleans; decimal integers without extra signs, leading zeros or whitespace; comma-separated sequence values and semicolon-separated groups. Whole-number medians have no decimal suffix; half medians use .5. Do not append a newline to the returned value. Preserve the explicitly named textual sentinels such as none or #. Input fixtures are bounded so the demonstrated arithmetic fits its named Rust types; satisfy the stated input preconditions before applying the algorithm.

String and character-grid fixtures use ASCII unless the lesson explicitly specifies Unicode scalar values.

A problem is a good match for Aho–Corasick when it asks for many-pattern search, filters, signature scanning. Here the concrete task is: Parse lowercase ASCII text and nonempty lowercase ASCII patterns. Count every pattern occurrence, including overlaps and simultaneous suffix matches. The visible input `text=ahishers patterns=[he,she,his,hers]` is an example, not a definition of the whole problem. Ask what operations the solution must support and what the input guarantees. Look for repeated prefix queries or pattern matching before choosing a trie or preprocessing; a one-off short search may not need either. The right choice follows from those guarantees, not from a familiar noun in the prompt.

The decisive invariant is: Add failure links to a trie so one scan reports all pattern suffixes ending at each position. Try to say why it applies to the task without quoting the implementation. Which fact becomes known after one update, and which possible answers remain? `String` algorithms compare symbols or prefixes, but a Rust `String` is UTF-8 bytes. State whether the task means bytes, scalar values, or grapheme clusters. If that claim cannot be maintained on a legal input, the pattern is wrong or one of its preconditions is missing. A counterexample is more useful than a vague warning: change one property of the sample, trace the first two steps, and identify the exact claim that fails.

Compare costs before committing. The advertised bound is O(text + matches + total patterns) time; identify the operation responsible for it and the extra memory it needs. Then compare a straightforward alternative: a direct scan, full sort, or repeated recomputation may be easier but can pay for the same work many times. Do not choose the more elaborate method just because it has a famous name. For the sample, predict `4` and explain which part of the state lets the method reach that result.

When the prompt is ambiguous, ask about input size, ordering, duplicates, and required output format. Test empty pattern and text, repeated characters, overlapping matches, and non-ASCII input if the contract allows it. Use bytes only when the input contract permits byte-wise matching. Never index a `String` as though every character occupied one byte. The Rust sketch can show a useful primitive without proving that the whole task is solved; connect each primitive to the requested output. You should be able to name a fitting case, a near miss, and the assumption separating them before writing the first line.
